segments.text: Governance theories provide different explanatory lenses for how society should be governed, and how institutions, individuals, markets, and communities jointly shape collective outcomes. The recommended revision tool, given explicitly in the syllabus, is an eight-column comparison across all theories: view of the state, view of the individual/community, role of the market, source of power, coordination method, a genuine strength, a genuine criticism, and a practical application — the goal throughout is
conceptual clarity, not ideological advocacy
for any one theory over the others.
Communitarian approaches emphasize that individuals are
socially embedded

— community bonds, shared values, and mutual social responsibilities matter alongside, not instead of, individual rights. Governance, on this view, should explicitly take collective bonds and shared community values into account, rather than treating governance purely as a matter of protecting individual rights and preferences in isolation from the surrounding community.
Decentered governance theory focuses on the
beliefs, traditions, and everyday practices of diverse actors
, rather than treating institutions as fixed structures that mechanically determine behaviour on their own. Its central insight: institutions genuinely influence behaviour, but actors continuously
interpret and reshape

those institutions through their own ongoing practice — governance is therefore never simply “given” by formal structure alone, but is continuously produced and reproduced through actors’ interpretive practice.
Libertarian socialist thought combines
opposition to concentrated coercive authority
(rejecting both authoritarian state control and, distinctively, unchecked private concentrations of economic power) with support for
cooperative or socially owned arrangements
, emphasizing decentralized self-management and voluntary association over both centralized state control and unregulated market hierarchy.
Institutionalism explains governance outcomes through formal rules, informal norms, historical paths, and organizational structures — with three distinguishable schools, worth naming precisely:

items.text: stresses path dependence — how past institutional choices constrain and shape what is feasible later (echoing the path-dependence point made about administrative reform theory in the Public Administration chapter).
stresses how institutions shape the incentives facing strategically self-interested actors.

stresses norms, identities, and culturally appropriate behaviour — actors follow institutional templates partly because doing so is seen as appropriate or legitimate, not only because it is individually advantageous.

segments.text: Marxist approaches analyse governance through
class relations, ownership, and power within the political economy

, generally viewing state institutions as shaped by (and reflecting) underlying economic structures and class conflicts, rather than as fully neutral arbiters standing above social interests. The analytical contribution worth naming precisely: Marxist analysis specifically
questions the claim that public institutions are fully neutral
between competing social interests — a genuinely distinct starting assumption from theories (like pluralist or institutionalist accounts) that treat the state as a more neutral arena.
Neoliberal governance emphasizes markets, competition, private enterprise, contracting, and a state role oriented more toward
enabling and regulating

than toward direct production of goods and services — directly connecting to the New Public Management approach already covered in the Public Administration chapter’s Unit I. Its acknowledged criticisms, worth stating as a genuine counterweight in any balanced answer, concern inequality (market coordination can produce or worsen unequal outcomes), the erosion of non-market public values, and market failure (markets do not automatically produce socially optimal outcomes in every context, particularly for public goods).

Rational choice theory explains behaviour by modelling actors as choosing among alternatives under specified incentives and constraints — directly paralleling Public Choice Theory from the Public Administration chapter’s Unit II, since public choice is essentially rational choice theory applied specifically to political and administrative actors. It is genuinely useful for analysing collective-action and principal-agent problems, but its acknowledged limitation, worth stating explicitly, is that it can oversimplify the role of values, identities, and bounded rationality (recall Herbert Simon’s concept from the Business Administration chapter) in actual human decision-making.

Regulation theory studies why and how public authorities create rules, standards, and oversight mechanisms for economic and social activity — asking specifically whose interests regulation actually serves, how compliance is actually produced, and why regulation sometimes fails. Central problems it examines include
regulatory capture
(the regulated industry unduly influencing its own regulator — already introduced in the Public Administration chapter’s Unit X),
information asymmetry
(regulators typically knowing less about the regulated activity than the regulated parties themselves do), and genuine
enforcement capacity
constraints, alongside the constant underlying balance between necessary protection and avoidably excessive regulatory burden.
Key takeaways for Unit II

items.text: Use the eight-column comparison (state, individual/community, market, power source, coordination, strength, criticism, application) systematically across all seven theories — this structural discipline, more than memorizing any one theory’s definition alone, is what this unit actually rewards.

Several theories here directly parallel concepts already introduced in the Public Administration chapter: neoliberalism parallels NPM, rational choice parallels public choice theory, and historical institutionalism’s path dependence parallels the reform-theory discussion — cross-referencing these connections strengthens an answer.

The unit’s explicit instruction is conceptual clarity, not advocacy — a strong answer states each theory’s genuine strength and genuine criticism, never presenting one theory as simply correct and the others as simply wrong.
